reasoning: Failure-driven edits (Group 1) are kept at priority. They act on distinct text regions: the clause-vote/prefix-check replacement of the odd-one-out bullet, the final-sanity prefix exception, the non-uniform 'some C' clarification, the hub-writing rule in step 8, the symmetry/equivariance test, the numerics-rider bullet and the equivalence-stem cue. Together they address the main failure pattern: defaulting to the bare or dropped-clause neighbour of the hub, or taking an inflated rider. Group 2 has a single success edit. It is a visible checklist that writes out quantifier skeletons, ranges and hypotheses and notes which finalists use each stem-defined symbol. It does not duplicate any failure edit, because it targets the Final sanity pass heading rather than the sentence the failure edit replaces. It also matches the optimizer memory's defined-term tie-break, so I kept it with light compression. No edits touch the SLOW_UPDATE block. Failure edits keep their original wording, apart from light compression of the success edit.

edits.target: - When options differ only by where a coefficient or index sits (λ on the s_1 term vs the s_2 term, A before B, i vs j), count how many options use each placement. If one option is the isolated swap and all others agree on the other placement, the swap is the corruption (distractors are single edits of the truth and so mostly inherit its details). Confirm with the stem's naming order or a limiting case (a parameter → 0) when possible.
edits.content:
- Clause vote (write it out before ranking): for each atomic clause (constant or dependence list, weight such as sum N_c vs sum c·N_c, level or index, range, coefficient/index placement such as λ on s_1 vs s_2, a 'Moreover' clause, a tail like 'need not' / 'only'), note each option's wording. Distractors are single edits of the truth, so the truth agrees with the majority on every clause. An option that is the lone dissenter where all the others agree (it alone drops the dependence list, changes a weight or placement, omits the 'Moreover' clause, or adds a 'need not' tail) is presumed corrupted; overturn this only by derivation. Confirm placement swaps with the stem's naming order or a limiting case (a parameter → 0). Position earns no credit: the bare, hedged or dependence-free variant is often listed last.
- Prefix check: if one option's text appears verbatim inside two or more others, it is their common weakening, not a safe base. Give each extension one cheap test (degenerate case, cheap invariant, does it silently change a stem hypothesis) and take the extension whose extras survive. An extra that contradicts an equality case (strict inequality on a plateau) or is only an 'asymptotic / for large indices' downgrade is the corrupted one. Keep the bare option only if every extension fails.
- Do not import a property (invariance under scaling, 'unique up to scaling / ray / normalization') from a better-known analogous invariant. Check it for the stem's own invariant. If the stem never normalizes the objects and homogeneity of degree 0 is not shown, state uniqueness plainly.

edits.target: If your choice carries the extra, more specific, or more elaborate clause and you only have a plausibility argument for it, switch to the plainer option unless that option is demonstrably false or strictly implied by a fully proved alternative.
edits.content: If your choice carries an extra clause that you cannot derive or that fails a test, switch to the plainer option. Do this only if the plainer option is not a verbatim prefix of two or more other options (then compare the extensions per the clause vote and take the one whose extras survive), and it is not demonstrably false or strictly implied by a fully proved alternative.

edits.target: Equally, a vague 'some C' is often a weakened distractor. Decide by checking against the stem, not by default.
edits.content: Equally, a vague 'some C' is often a weakened distractor. In an 'equivalent to' stem whose target inequality has one fixed constant, 'for every u ... there exists C>0' lets C depend on u (non-uniform, nearly vacuous) and cannot be equivalent. The faithful option names a constant depending only on the stem's structural parameters (e.g. C=C(p,q,n)) and keeps the stem's exponents, norms and ranges. If the other options all state the dependence list, the lone option omitting it is the weakened one.

edits.target: Override the hub only on positive evidence.
edits.content: Override the hub only on positive evidence. WRITE THE HUB OUT before ranking: name it, then label every other option 'hub + X', 'hub - X' or 'hub with X swapped'. ADD-neighbours look stronger (a rider). DROP-neighbours look safer (one direction of an iff, bare membership, 'only / non-uniform / XP-only' hedges). SWAP-neighbours change a range, object or direction. A superlative in the stem ('strongest', 'exact', 'complete') is NOT evidence against the hub: the hub is already the strongest statement the source proves. Leave the hub only if (i) an ADD-neighbour's extra clause is a standard consequence you can derive in a few lines from the stem's own hypotheses AND is not a coefficient/rate/expansion, a stronger notion of equivalence, a new object, a weakened hypothesis, or a changed quantifier/range; or (ii) you pick a DROP-neighbour because the hub contains a clause that fails a concrete test. If two options are equivalent under the stem's ranges, the hub is the one written in the notation the other options edit.

edits.target: Do not add a ray clause unless the invariant is scale-invariant.
edits.content: - Symmetry/equivariance: an option upgrading 'isomorphic' to 'isomorphic compatibly with the projection, group action, labelling, basepoint or orientation' (equivariant, canonical, over the base) is a rider unless the stem asks for it. Test it with a trivial symmetry of the data (relabel by an automorphism of the coefficients, flip a sign, Galois-conjugate, reparametrize): the plain-isomorphism statement survives, the structure-preserving one fails.

edits.target: - Options with specific numerics (explicit asymptotic coefficients, exact constants, extra sign or monotonicity claims, a 'moreover' clause on large-time behaviour) are the typical inflated distractors. Keep one only if you can derive the extra detail.
edits.content: - Options with specific numerics (explicit asymptotic coefficients, exact constants, extra sign or monotonicity claims, a 'moreover' clause on large-time behaviour) are the typical inflated distractors. Keep one only if you can derive the extra detail in a few lines. An 'in addition / moreover / as λ→0' tail that attaches a coefficient, expansion, rate, sign claim or asymptotic-closeness bound to an existence, regularity or membership theorem is a rider. It is NOT the 'explicit formula for the quantity the stem names' upgrade, which applies only when the stem asks for the value or formula of that quantity. 'Even without [a stem hypothesis]' is always the corruption, however strong it looks.

edits.target: ## Trivial directions, negative hedges, iff vs one-way, FPT vs XP
edits.content: - Equivalence stems: the true equivalent sits at the same level as the stem's own object and is phrased in the stem's vocabulary. An option that shifts the level or index (k → k+1, a higher class), introduces newly named subobjects as a 'criterion', or restates the stem's own hypothesis as part of the conclusion is an inflated reformulation. Take it only if you can derive both directions.

edits.target: ## Final sanity pass (do this before committing)
edits.content: Visible check: write each finalist's quantifier skeleton (e.g. 'for all eps, exists C, for all N>=2, exists b'), parameter range, domain and hypotheses beside the stem's, and note which finalists use each symbol or term the stem defines (a tie-break signal, not an absolute). A finalist that reorders quantifiers, narrows or extends the range, relaxes or negates a stem hypothesis, or contains a rider that contradicts a stem definition or makes another clause of the same option vacuous or contradictory is the corruption. Discard it before any strength ranking. Among the rest, take the one whose every extra clause you can derive.
